analysis.one_liner: Restricts smart speakers and video doorbells from recording without consent, enforced by the FTC and states.
analysis.headline: The bill to stop smart speakers and doorbells from recording without consent never got a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it unlawful for companies that run smart speakers like Alexa or Google Home to store or share recordings of speech unless the device was deliberately activated by a wake word and the user was told, agreed to a specific purpose, and can delete recordings anytime. It applies similar rules to video doorbells like Ring and Nest, and lets the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general enforce the rules, with fines up to $40,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits: The millions of people who own smart speakers or video doorbells gain more control over recordings of their home conversations and front-door activity, and anyone whose voice or image gets captured by a neighbor's always-listening device gains limits on how those recordings are stored or shared. People who no longer work with their voice recordings handed to human reviewers or third parties without clear consent also gain.

how_it_helps.text: Smart speaker providers could not store recordings or transcripts of speech unless the device was specifically activated by a wake word the user knows, and the device had to give an audible or visual signal when activated.

Any use or sharing of recordings beyond processing a request or improving the voice system requires clear notice at setup, express consent for that specific purpose, and a right for the user to delete recordings at any time.

Video doorbell providers could only record when the button is pressed, the built-in motion sensor detects someone, or a remote user activates it, and the recording must be delivered to the user's phone in real time.

The Federal Trade Commission would treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue to stop violations, force compliance, or collect civil penalties up to $40,000 per violation.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that sell and operate smart speakers and video doorbells — Amazon, Google, Apple, and the home security firms behind Ring, Nest, and SimpliSafe — would lose a source of data they can use to improve products and build other services, and would face FTC and state enforcement costs. Consumers would pay indirectly through slower product improvement and possibly higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Smart speaker and home security companies

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to proprietary smart speakers and video doorbells, leaving other always-on internet-connected devices such as phones, TVs, and security cameras outside its scope, so a person's protections would depend on which device is listening.

Restricting how companies store and use voice data could slow the improvement of speech recognition and voice features that many users rely on, and companies would carry new compliance and enforcement costs that could show up in product prices.

The recording limits depend on the device detecting a wake word known to the user, and the definition of a video doorbell is narrow, so coverage of different device designs may leave gaps an enforcement agency would have to argue through case by case.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and narrow: it targets two specific categories of home devices that have drawn well-documented complaints about recordings of people without meaningful consent, and it gives users a deletion right and enforcers real penalties. The cost is also narrow — reduced flexibility for device makers and some friction in product features — and the main honest objection is that the bill covers only two product types while the underlying privacy issue spans many more devices. As a targeted consumer protection, the benefits clearly outweigh the costs for the devices it does cover.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Seth Moulton (D-MA) introduced the bill on July 25, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
The next day it was referred to the subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, and no further action was ever taken on the bill.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor during the entire two-year life of the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that operate smart speakers and video doorbells are better off, since the recording and consent limits never took effect; consumers are no better off than before, with no federal baseline for these devices.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no record of how parties stood on it.

industries.note: The bill would bar storing voice recordings except after deliberate activation and would require notice, specific consent, and deletion rights for any other use of the data. Voice data helps these companies improve speech recognition and develop services, so the bill would remove a data source and expose them to FTC and state enforcement.

industries.industry: Video doorbell and home security companies (Ring, Nest, SimpliSafe)
industries.note: The bill would limit when doorbells can record and what companies can do with the footage beyond showing it to the user in real time. Some of these firms have drawn attention for sharing footage with third parties, and the bill would cut off that practice and its revenue potential.

The bill prohibits transmitting voice or video recordings to third parties without express consent for a specific purpose, reducing the pool of home audio and video data that can be marketed or used for ad targeting.
